facts.label: How billing works
facts.value: Classic lists monthly prices: Hobby $46, Startup $99, Business $299 before the displayed promotion, and custom Enterprise. Pricing shows $; Terms say payments may be in USD or euros plus VAT, without showing how a buyer’s currency is selected.

facts.label: How billing works
facts.value: The pricing page displays Business at $149.50/month for 12 months as 50% off its $299/month price, “until Dec 15.” It does not name the year.

facts.label: How billing works
facts.value: The early-stage offer advertises 40% off Startup for up to one year for companies with fewer than four employees, funding up to $300,000, and age under two years. At the published $99 list price, the discount would be $59.40/month.

facts.label: How billing works
facts.value: Terms describe a subscription term usually lasting one month, automatic renewal and payment in advance. Customer cancellation stops the next renewal; the Terms do not promise refunds for already billed periods.

facts.label: How billing works
facts.value: Terms mention credit-card payment, USD or EUR and extra VAT. The checked public pricing page displays monthly prices but does not identify card type, annual prepayment, an annual discount, or a separate minimum commitment.

facts.label: How billing works
facts.value: Next Pro is listed at $15 per member per month. The pricing page says customers pay only for administrators who manage the service, but it does not define billable administrator roles, a minimum seat count or a separate annual rate.

facts.label: Ongoing free plan
facts.value: Next Free is advertised as free forever. It includes two team members, five monitoring checks, one public page, 500 subscribers, no custom domain, one monitoring region, RSS/Slack/email notifications and no incident automation.

facts.label: Ongoing free plan
facts.value: Classic’s main plan list starts at Hobby for $46/month. A separate Heroku add-on panel advertises a free alpha offer with two team members, one monitored service and 50 subscriptions, and says only three add-ons remain. Whether that limited offer can still be claimed is not established.

facts.label: Ongoing free plan
facts.value: Classic paid-plan limits are published, but no general ongoing free plan for the regular Classic service is listed. A 14-day trial is separately advertised.

facts.label: Trial
facts.value: Classic advertises a 14-day trial with no credit card and access to all core features. The public Terms do not explain whether adding a card during a trial triggers a charge or spell out a separate trial conversion rule.

facts.label: Trial
facts.value: Next has a Free plan and a “Start free” link, but no separate paid-plan trial duration, card requirement or auto-charge rule was found in its plan page or Next docs.

facts.label: Smallest useful paid plan
facts.value: For a Classic page on a custom domain, Startup is the lowest public plan with one custom domain: $99/month, 20 managing members, 1,000 subscribers/viewer members, 30 services, 15 metrics, two languages and 300-day incident retention. Hobby lists zero custom domains.

facts.label: Smallest useful paid plan
facts.value: Next Pro is $15/member/month and lists 20 checks, five public or private pages, unlimited subscribers, two custom domains, IP/auth access, incident automation and unlimited check regions.

facts.label: When a limit is exceeded
facts.value: Next publishes five checks and one page on Free, and 20 checks/five pages on Pro, but its pricing page and Next docs do not say whether excess checks/pages are blocked, whether an upgrade is required, or whether overages are billed.

facts.label: When a limit is exceeded
facts.value: Classic publishes subscriber, member, service, metric, language, domain and retention limits, but the pricing page, FAQ and checked service/account docs do not explain blocking, upgrade prompts or overage charges at the cap.

facts.label: Bill controls
facts.value: No public guide was found that documents a hard spending cap, usage alert that stops charges, or per-project billing ceiling for Classic.

facts.label: Bill controls
facts.value: Next’s plan page and docs list fixed included limits but do not describe usage-based billing alerts or a hard spending cap.

facts.label: Data retention
facts.value: Classic plan comparison gives incident-history retention of 90 days for Hobby, 300 days for Startup, and unlimited for Business and Enterprise. A separate setting can hide public incident history after a chosen display period without deleting the incidents.

facts.label: Data retention
facts.value: Next status pages show a rolling uptime graph for 30, 60 or 90 days and a history of past notices. The docs do not state a fixed retention period for underlying incidents or check results.

facts.label: Data retention
facts.value: Terms state that web-server access logs are kept for no more than 24 hours. Privacy policy says personal information is kept only as long as needed for the service, law or legal claims; it does not give a general fixed duration.

facts.label: People, apps and projects
facts.value: Classic plan limits are 5/20/50/custom managing team members, 500/1,000/4,000/custom subscriptions and matching viewer-member allowances, 10/30/100/custom monitored services, and 5/15/50/custom metrics. The FAQ says organizations have unlimited status pages, with a separate subscription per organization.

facts.label: People, apps and projects
facts.value: Classic has page-level and organization-level memberships. Owner, Admin, Editor, Billing and Viewer roles are documented; viewer members do not consume managing-team seats and use the subscription/viewer allowance.

facts.label: People, apps and projects
facts.value: Next Free allows two team members; Pro lists unlimited team members and is billed per member. Free includes one public page and 500 subscribers; Pro has five public or private pages and unlimited subscribers.

facts.label: People, apps and projects
facts.value: The page plans name subscriber capacities but the checked Classic FAQ and subscription docs do not say whether these caps apply per page or across an organization.

facts.label: Home region and eligible buyers
facts.value: The listed company is based in Berlin, Germany. Classic terms say paid services are supplied to an “Entrepreneur”; the same site advertises Hobby for individuals and has consumer-rights language. Buyer eligibility is not consistently described.

facts.label: Jobs it covers
facts.value: Primary job: publish public or private service-status pages and send incident or maintenance notices. It also offers URL monitoring, incident automation and internal incident coordination. The page communicates service health; monitoring checks are the detection function.

facts.label: Hosted and self-hosted options
facts.value: StatusPal Classic is vendor-hosted. Its docs describe hosted pages, vendor monitoring and vendor-managed status-page infrastructure; no complete self-host installation path was located.

facts.label: Hosted and self-hosted options
facts.value: StatusPal Next is presented as a hosted service with a vendor login, public service-status page and hosted docs. No self-host package or installation guide was located.

facts.label: Languages and frameworks
facts.value: No application SDK or code instrumentation is required for the status-page service: Classic checks a URL and Next checks HTTP, HTTPS or TCP endpoints.

facts.label: Alert channels and costs
facts.value: Classic docs show subscriber notifications via email, SMS, Slack, Microsoft Teams and Google Chat, among other channels. Pricing shows channel rows only as marks that do not reveal their tier placement in text; the docs and checked integration pages do not map every channel to a plan or give message prices.

facts.label: Alert channels and costs
facts.value: Next Free lists RSS, Slack and email; Pro adds SMS. Next monitoring also sends direct failure and recovery alerts to selected team members. No SMS credit, third-party carrier charge, delivery cap or extra channel price is stated.

facts.label: Alert channels and costs
facts.value: Classic plan cards list external-service status as a feature on Startup, Business and Enterprise, not Hobby. The pricing matrix’s integration checkmarks do not reveal the plan gates for all email, metrics or incident-response integrations.

facts.label: Alert noise and escalation
facts.value: Classic monitoring alerts after a URL returns a non-2xx status for more than five minutes; a recovered service closes its automated incident after it has been up for at least two minutes. Checks can pause during scheduled maintenance.

facts.label: Alert noise and escalation
facts.value: Classic custom incident types can define escalation and de-escalation to other types. This changes incident severity; it is not a documented automatic alert-retry rule.

facts.label: Alert noise and escalation
facts.value: Classic subscription groups let an operator send selected incident or maintenance notices to a subset of subscribers; subscribers can also filter by service and incident type.

facts.label: Alert noise and escalation
facts.value: Next monitoring sends alerts when a check fails or recovers and can create/resolve an incident automatically. The checked Next docs do not state retries, failure grouping, repeated-alert cadence, acknowledgement timeout or routing rules.

facts.label: Alert noise and escalation
facts.value: Classic status-page admins can configure alerts for incidents that remain open too long, and subscribers can filter which services or incident types they follow. Exact plan availability for these features is not stated.

facts.label: Deployment fit
facts.value: Classic monitoring checks a customer-provided URL using an HTTP method and headers. Private endpoints, intranet access, agent installation, and named cloud-host compatibility are not described in the monitoring guide.

facts.label: Deployment fit
facts.value: Next supports URL checks over HTTP, HTTPS or TCP. A check can run from the US, EU or both. The docs do not name support for private networks, browser flows, mobile apps or specific cloud platforms.

facts.label: Sending data in
facts.value: Classic accepts URL check results and can create incidents from an external monitor through email/metrics integrations; its API and incident automation can update status-page incidents. It is not documented as a log, trace or error-event ingestion service.

facts.label: Sending data in
facts.value: Classic can receive status changes from external monitors through inbound email or incoming webhooks, including a custom JSONPath mapping for other webhook formats. Legacy inbound email searches for down and up; the docs call webhooks newer and more reliable.

facts.label: Sending data in
facts.value: Next supports scheduled HTTP/HTTPS/TCP health checks and incoming webhooks for status-page updates. No logs, traces, OTLP or application-error ingestion endpoint was found in the Next docs checked.

facts.label: Setup path
facts.value: Classic setup is to create a status page and services, enter a URL/method/optional headers for a monitored service, choose recipients, then optionally enable automatic incident creation and a response-time chart.

facts.label: Setup path
facts.value: For an external Classic monitor, create a service, enable inbound or webhook monitoring, then configure the monitor to send an email or webhook to the generated address. The help guide says a service cannot use StatusPal monitoring and third-party monitoring at the same time.

facts.label: Setup path
facts.value: Next setup starts with creating an organization/page, then adding a scheduled check with endpoint, protocol/method, timeout, region and recipients; optional page automation links the check to a service.

facts.label: Check types
facts.value: Classic out-of-the-box monitoring accepts a ping URL and configurable HTTP method and headers. The guide does not list TCP, DNS, browser-flow, keyword or authenticated-check types.

facts.label: Check types
facts.value: Next supports HTTP, HTTPS or TCP endpoint checks with a configurable HTTP method. The docs do not list DNS, browser actions, keyword assertions or certificate-expiry checks as check types.

facts.label: Check frequency and timeout
facts.value: Classic checks once per minute; it notifies after a non-2xx result persists for more than five minutes. The docs do not state a request timeout value.

facts.label: Check frequency and timeout
facts.value: Next checks run “on a schedule,” with a configurable response timeout of 1–60 seconds. The checked pricing and monitoring docs do not state the schedule interval or plan-specific interval range.

facts.label: Probe locations and check counting
facts.value: Classic privacy offers an EU or US server choice for status-page hosting, but Classic monitoring docs do not identify probe locations, location count per check or run-billing rules.

facts.label: Probe locations and check counting
facts.value: Next checks can run from the US, EU or both. Free includes one region and Pro lists unlimited regions; docs do not state whether multi-region checks consume multiple check allotments or how many probe locations exist within each region.

facts.label: Failure confirmation and maintenance
facts.value: Classic reports a failure after more than five minutes of non-2xx responses, resolves an automated incident after at least two minutes back up, and can ignore failures during a scheduled maintenance window.

facts.label: Failure confirmation and maintenance
facts.value: Next alerts on check failure and recovery and optionally creates/resolves a status incident. Its monitoring guide does not specify retry count, quorum, consecutive-failure threshold or maintenance-window pause behavior.

facts.label: Certificate and domain expiry
facts.value: No public Classic or Next docs checked describe TLS certificate-expiry warnings, domain-expiry reminders or DNS-expiry monitoring. Custom-domain setup and automatic SSL provisioning are described, but those are not expiry alerts.

facts.label: Status-page limits and branding
facts.value: Classic permits unlimited pages within an organization according to the FAQ. Pricing lists page access as public on Hobby and public/private on Startup, Business and Enterprise; custom domains are 0/1/4/custom, and incident retention is 90/300 days/unlimited/unlimited.

facts.label: Status-page limits and branding
facts.value: Next Free includes one public page, 500 subscribers, no custom domains and public access. Pro includes five public or private pages, unlimited subscribers, two custom domains, IP/auth access, and customizable branding controls in docs.

facts.label: Status-page limits and branding
facts.value: Legacy Classic custom-domain configurations will eventually need to move to the current custom-domain setup. The guide gives no migration deadline.

facts.label: Status-page limits and branding
facts.value: Classic docs describe public/private pages, custom domains with managed SSL, CSS/HTML customization, an uptime calendar and audience access groups. Access groups let private-page viewers see only assigned services. The pricing feature matrix lists audience-specific pages for Enterprise, but does not make the relationship to access groups clear.

facts.label: Status-page limits and branding
facts.value: Classic supports more than ten languages; current plan cards list one, two, three or custom status-page languages. AI auto-translation is documented as Business and above.

facts.label: Subscriber notifications
facts.value: Classic subscriber limits are 500, 1,000, 4,000 and custom; the plan table says private-page viewer-member allowances match subscription counts. The scope of counts per page vs organization is not stated.

facts.label: Subscriber notifications
facts.value: Next Free includes 500 subscribers; Pro says unlimited. Visitors can subscribe to a page and filter notices by service; documented channels include email, Slack and RSS on the page docs, while pricing lists SMS on Pro.

facts.label: Subscriber notifications
facts.value: Classic docs describe notification filters, subscription groups and automatic maintenance notices, and show email, SMS, Slack, Microsoft Teams and Google Chat. Pricing marks do not disclose all channel or feature gates; extra message costs and country restrictions were not found.

facts.label: Subscriber notifications
facts.value: Next monitoring alerts selected team recipients directly on failure/recovery. Status-page subscribers receive a notice only when the check is connected to status-page automation; Slack-based incident management is a separate team workflow.

facts.label: Status update source
facts.value: Classic supports manual incident and maintenance updates, internal monitoring that can create/resolve incidents, third-party integrations and API updates. Its plan comparison lists incident retention separately by tier.

facts.label: Status update source
facts.value: Next supports manual incidents and notices, automated status changes from its own checks, and incoming webhooks from external tools. Incident Management can coordinate responders and runbooks separately from the subscriber-facing notice.

facts.label: Status update source
facts.value: Classic incidents can be created, updated, escalated, de-escalated and resolved; maintenance has scheduled, started, optional monitoring and completed states. Each update can notify subscribers.

facts.label: Status update source
facts.value: StatusPal’s own public service-status page currently lists Classic in EU/US and Next’s dashboard, API, monitoring, notifications and status pages as operational. Its latest visible notices are security updates dated October 23 and 27, 2026.

facts.label: Export and deletion
facts.value: The FAQ documents permanent account deletion. Terms say deleted content may remain in systems or backups for some period, and access logs are removed within 24 hours. A full status-page export format and limits were not found in the checked public docs.

facts.label: Export and deletion
facts.value: Next DPA says StatusPal will delete personal data within ten business days after service cessation, subject to the agreement. The Next docs checked do not give a full export format or a self-service deletion schedule for check results.

facts.label: Sensitive-data controls
facts.value: StatusPal collects subscriber contact data, including email addresses and phone numbers. Terms make the customer responsible for its own subscriber-data collection and privacy notice; privacy policy lists personal and usage data.

facts.label: Sensitive-data controls
facts.value: No masking, secret-redaction or request-header filtering rules for monitored endpoint responses were found in Classic monitoring docs, Next monitoring docs, Terms or Privacy. Classic permits custom request headers, but the docs do not explain how credentials are stored or masked.

facts.label: Storage regions and data terms
facts.value: Classic Privacy says customers may choose a U.S. or EU server for hosting a status page and associated personal-data transfer. The DPA confirms the selected EU or U.S. server; subprocessors may access/process data globally.

facts.label: Storage regions and data terms
facts.value: Next publishes US/EU monitoring locations, but Next’s docs, Privacy Policy and DPA do not clearly say whether Next data can select those storage regions or whether the Classic EU/US choice applies to Next.

facts.label: Product identity
facts.value: StatusPal; current products are StatusPal Classic and StatusPal Next. No former product name was listed.

facts.label: Availability and product changes
facts.value: The linked product changelog showed Next updates through 2026-10-19 and a Classic update on 2026-10-01, consistent with current work on both editions.

facts.label: Availability and product changes
facts.value: Classic is the edition used by existing paying customers and is described as supported indefinitely, with no required migration. New features are directed to Next.

facts.label: Availability and product changes
facts.value: Next has its own published Free and Pro plans, current docs and a separate service listing; the February 2026 announcement described some Next modules as beta or in progress at that time. The current plan page and docs show them as available now.

facts.label: Availability and ownership
facts.value: The About page identifies E.M. StatusPal UG (haftungsbeschränkt), in Berlin, Germany, as the company. No acquisition announcement was found in the official blog or announcements checked.

facts.value: Classic has a public docs site and help center, with support contact through support@statuspal.io. Pricing shows Priority support, Phone support and Custom SLA only as marks whose plan assignments are not legible in the extracted table.

facts.label: Help and documentation
facts.value: Next has a public documentation section, roadmap, changelog link and contact email. No support response time or support-tier terms were found on the Next pricing and docs pages checked.

facts.label: Hosted delivery
facts.value: Vendor runs checks, pulse receivers, dashboard/API and status pages; clients access a hosted service.

facts.label: SMS scope and country caveat
facts.value: SMS limited to important down/up and SSL-invalid/recovery alerts; no still-down SMS reminders. Sender IDs/providers vary by country/carrier; guide says delivery cannot be guaranteed.

facts.label: Webhook delivery limits
facts.value: POST event arrays; recipient must return 2xx; errors retried up to 25 times over several days; warning after sustained 10/100/900 failures; endpoint removed after 1,000 failed deliveries.

facts.label: Confirmation, repeats and muting
facts.value: Failure/recovery require 3 matching results, including at least 2 locations. Still-down reminder after 60 down checks, then growing delays; reminder schedule not configurable. API mute until time/recovery/forever.

facts.label: Native escalation
facts.value: Acknowledgement-driven notification escalation is still an Open request; no native on-call rotation/acknowledgement policy established in current guides.

facts.label: Public and internal fit
facts.value: Public HTTP/TCP/ICMP endpoints can be checked without installing an agent. Pulse monitors internal/private systems by outbound HTTPS calls to the vendor.

facts.label: Data paths
facts.value: Vendor polling for protocol checks; HTTPS GET/HEAD/POST to secret pulse endpoint, optional POST body; management HTTPS JSON API and outgoing POST webhooks.

facts.label: Setup
facts.value: Create account, add authorized URL/check type and interval, configure selected locations/assertions/auth and recipients; enable public report/page if needed. For pulse, create named check/duration and send completion request to secret URL.

facts.label: Protocols and HTTP methods
facts.value: HTTP, HTTPS, TCP, TCPS and ICMP plus pulse; HTTP defaults GET/HEAD, with POST/PUT/PATCH/DELETE/OPTIONS and optional request body/custom headers.

facts.label: HTTP assertion rules
facts.value: Contains numeric 100–599 selects expected HTTP code; other UTF-8 text searches response body, ignoring HTTP status. String max 1,000 bytes; only first 1 MB searched; whitespace normalized; redirects followed.

facts.label: TCP open/closed and TLS behavior
facts.value: TCP/TCPS test connect acceptance; optional banner string. Since August 2026, Contains <closed> accepts connection refusal/timeout and alerts on open port; DNS errors still alert. Invalid TCPS cert generates warning separately from TCP uptime.

facts.label: Check intervals
facts.value: Regular check choices 15/30/60/120/300/600/1800/3600 seconds; API create default 60 seconds. Same public interface applies during credits trial and prepaid use.

facts.label: Timeouts
facts.value: TCP connection 10 seconds; TLS handshake shares that 10-second delay; HTTP/TCP response wait 30 seconds.

facts.label: Current probe inventory
facts.value: 10 listed nodes: Los Angeles, Miami, Toronto, Roubaix, Frankfurt, Cape Town, Helsinki, Singapore, Tokyo and Sydney; IPv4/IPv6 addresses listed.

facts.label: Selection and single-location exception
facts.value: API disabled_locations excludes named probes; normal UI requires at least 2. Operator's later 2021 reply offers support-enabled per-account bypass for single-location monitoring.

facts.label: Counting and multi-location execution
facts.value: Pricing says 1 credit per check and dual-stack same price, but exact scheduling across selected probes and the credit treatment of extra failure/recovery requests are not fully defined.

facts.label: Failure confirmation
facts.value: Two extra Down verifications, at least one different location, for three Down results total; verifications run at half the configured interval. Same three-Up confirmation for recovery since 2024-02-26.

facts.label: Maintenance and mute
facts.value: No built-in maintenance scheduler per current guide. Manually/API disable and re-enable checks; external checks stop and status freezes at last known value. Mute-until timestamp/recovery/forever suppresses alerts while recording monitoring.

facts.label: SSL warning windows
facts.value: Expiry notifications 30/14/7/1 days before expiration, 10am in account timezone; 30-day notice skipped for short (~3-month) certs. Invalid/recovered certs have distinct webhook events.

facts.label: Domain expiry
facts.value: RDAP/WHOIS expiry lookup and optional domain-expiration webhook at 14/7/1 days; operator says expired domain still returning HTTP 200 is not automatically marked Down solely for expiry.

facts.label: Pages and branding

facts.label: Page/component caps and fees

facts.label: Privacy/access options

facts.label: Subscriber support

facts.label: Interval schedule and grace
facts.value: Pulse duration from 15 seconds to about 1 month plus a few days; natural-language durations accepted. Missed signal after duration means Down; grace folded into duration, e.g. daily task uses 26 hours.

facts.label: Monthly rule and irregular cron
facts.value: A duration such as 1 month 2 hours schedules expected next pulse same day next month; last-day pulses expect next month's last day. Irregular cron expressions are Under Review, operator says not implemented.

facts.label: Failure, output and payload validation
facts.value: Missing pulse causes Down; successful pulse restores Up. GET/HEAD/POST accepted; optional POST body stored and visible around downtime. Since April 2026 required body string can mark received pulse Down if absent/no body.

facts.value: No documented distinct start/success run correlation, start-specific runtime timer, automatic exit-code capture or numeric per-pulse payload/history cap established.

facts.label: Ongoing free use

facts.label: Capacity and charging limits
facts.value: Private Actions usage can be blocked when allowance is exhausted without a payment method; with a payment method, extra usage is payable unless an applicable stopping budget blocks it.

facts.label: API and page limits

facts.label: Optional Globalping limits
facts.value: Upptime docs state 250 tests/hour/IP unauthenticated or 500/hour with a token; shared cloud-runner IPs may hit the allowance sooner.

facts.label: Bill controls
facts.value: GitHub supports scoped metered-product budgets with optional Stop usage when budget limit is reached. Alert-only budgets do not stop usage; threshold alerts can be set at 75%, 90% and 100%.

facts.label: Monitor and incident retention
facts.value: Response-time/status data is stored in files and git revision history; incidents are GitHub Issues. No fixed Upptime searchable/archive retention duration or paid extension is published.

facts.label: Short incident deletion
facts.value: Resolved incidents open for less than 15 minutes are deleted by default rather than retained as closed issues. Set skipDeleteIssues: true to retain them.

facts.label: Workflow operational records
facts.value: GitHub workflow logs/artifacts default to 90 days. Configurable range: 1–90 days public, 1–400 days private, subject to parent policies; changes apply to newly created records.

facts.label: People and endpoints
facts.value: No Upptime licensed seat/site cap; sites are listed in YAML. One repository config defines the instance/page, with global or per-site GitHub issue assignees and repository-based collaboration.

facts.label: Home region
facts.value: Maintainer/project home country and a vendor legal address are not published in the checked Upptime product, repository, FAQ and security pages.

facts.label: Eligibility
facts.value: MIT grant is to any person, including commercial software use. GitHub account use has separate terms, including minimum age 13 and applicable use restrictions.

facts.label: Jobs it covers
facts.value: External uptime/response-time checks, monitor-driven status pages, GitHub issue incidents and operator notifications.

facts.label: Deployment options
facts.value: Complete service is operated through your GitHub repository, Actions workflows, Issues and Pages. Standard hosted Linux runners or compatible Linux self-hosted runners can perform checks.

facts.label: Language SDKs
facts.value: No application instrumentation SDK is required for external checks. Monitored apps can use any stack reachable through supported checks; Upptime itself uses TypeScript and Svelte/Sapper packages.

facts.label: Notification channels
facts.value: Slack, Telegram, Discord, Zulip, Microsoft Teams, Gotify, custom webhooks, email and SMS integrations are documented.

facts.label: Delivery credits and rates
facts.value: No Upptime-included email/SMS/call credit balance, destination-country SMS tariff or provider-number rental cost is published in the notification/FAQ/setup docs.

facts.label: Noise, routing and recovery
facts.value: Down/degraded and recovery notifications accompany incident changes. Global/per-site assignees route GitHub issues; message templates are customizable. Multiple configurations of a provider support fallback, roundrobin (default) or no-fallback.

facts.label: Advanced escalation
facts.value: A timed escalation tree, acknowledgement timer, repeat-reminder schedule and per-target quiet-hours policy are not published in the checked notification/configuration/trigger guides.

facts.label: Deployment and private targets
facts.value: Default ubuntu-latest GitHub runner; compatible Linux self-hosted runners supported, including a documented ARM64 label example. Windows self-hosted runners are unsupported due to bundled node-libcurl.

facts.label: Data-input scope
facts.value: Normal operation actively polls endpoints and reads/writes GitHub data. workflow_dispatch/repository dispatch can trigger checks; it is not a documented OTLP, syslog, application-error or job-heartbeat ingestion endpoint.

facts.label: Setup path
facts.value: Create a template-derived GitHub repository including all branches; enable workflows; configure Pages from gh-pages; grant a scoped GitHub App token or PAT; set owner/repo/sites and notification secrets in configuration.

facts.label: Checks and assertions
facts.value: HTTP methods, custom headers/body, expected status codes, body text/regex checks and response-time thresholds; local TCP connect and TCP response-body checks; release source also includes WebSocket and SSL checks.

facts.label: Authentication and remote integration
facts.value: Headers/body can substitute allowlisted secrets, supporting token-authenticated API requests. Optional Globalping provides remote HTTP/PING checks; POST, local TCP-body checks and WebSocket checks are not supported through that path.

facts.label: Frequency
facts.value: Default and documented minimum scheduled interval 300 seconds; configurable POSIX cron via workflowSchedule.uptime. Current response-time snapshot schedule is daily, separately from five-minute health checks.

facts.label: Timeouts
facts.value: v1.46.5 local HTTP defaults: connect timeout 30 seconds, overall request timeout 60 seconds; configurable connectTimeout/requestTimeout. TCP response-read doc default is 10 seconds. Explicit Globalping timeout accepts 15, 20 or 30 seconds.

facts.label: Origins
facts.value: Default requests originate at the chosen Actions runner; location is not a named fixed probe city. Self-host runner network is operator-selected. Optional Globalping accepts location filters for country/city/continent/ASN/ISP/cloud region, including own tagged probes.

facts.label: Check counting and multiple regions
facts.value: v1.46.5 Globalping measurement requests limit: 1 and reads one result. To compare distinct regions, configure separate location-specific sites/instances; no native geographic quorum or per-location Upptime charge is documented.

facts.label: Confirmation retries
facts.value: If a site is down/degraded, v1.46.5 rechecks after 2 seconds, then 10 seconds if still failing; an up result stops confirmation. Local HTTP also has an inner default three total curl attempts for transient HTTP-0/network failures, with 1-second then 2-second backoff.

facts.label: Maintenance
facts.value: Release source reads open maintenance-labeled issues with start/end metadata and expectedDown/expectedDegraded site-slug lists. During the active interval, expected matching failures do not create a new outage issue; completed maintenance issues are closed.

facts.label: Certificate and domain expiry
facts.value: Release check: ssl marks certificate status down when expiry is missing/invalid or less than seven days away; seven or more days is up. Local and Globalping certificate paths are present.

facts.label: Certificate and domain expiry
facts.value: No native domain-registration expiry/RDAP reminder or DNS-expiry notice window found in the checked config, check-type interface and monitor source.

facts.label: Page, domains and branding
facts.value: One generated status website per configured repository; multiple endpoints have history views. Custom CNAME or GitHub Pages project path, logo/title/navigation/CSS/themes and footer text can be configured.

facts.label: Private publication
facts.value: Default private repositories do not publish a status site; config allows explicit publish: true. FAQ/setup require an authenticated API proxy to read private repository data for a working published site.

facts.label: Subscriber notifications
facts.value: GitHub repository watching and issue subscriptions can notify GitHub users through their chosen GitHub/email settings. Upptime's own configured channels alert operators.

facts.label: Customer subscribers and credits
facts.value: No native customer opt-in/unsubscribe list, 100/1,000/10,000 subscriber allowance, per-delivery tariff or subscriber-list export found in the checked status/configuration/notification/FAQ docs.

facts.label: Status updates and history
facts.value: Monitor failures open issues; recovery closes them. Operators add investigation/postmortem comments; issues are locked to team members by default. The public status page reads GitHub data and shows incident/history views.

facts.label: Dependencies
facts.value: GitHub repository, Actions, Issues/API and optionally Pages; Linux runner compatible with native node-libcurl, repository-write token and network access. Default hosted runner avoids managing a separate persistent application server/database.

facts.label: Sizing
facts.value: No workload-qualified Upptime CPU/RAM/disk minimum or recommendation found for 5/25/100 monitored endpoints in setup/config/package docs.

facts.label: Export
facts.value: Git files/revision history can be copied with a mirror backup. GitHub APIs/migration tools handle additional repository metadata; plain git history does not contain incident comments or all platform records.

facts.label: Deletion
facts.value: Owner/admin can delete the GitHub repository. Public forks remain; some deleted repositories can be restored within 90 days. No Upptime-specific physical-backup purge SLA is published.

facts.label: Secrets and publication
facts.value: Use GitHub repository secrets for target URLs, headers, bodies and provider credentials. The explicit top-level secrets list is authoritative, including an empty list; omitted list uses finite automatic compatibility references.

facts.label: Output redaction limits
facts.value: v1.46.5 redacts variable references in notification URLs, but source also logs site.url and writes it to incident/history templates. No universal response-body/PII masking policy is documented.

facts.label: Storage region and data terms
facts.value: No independent Upptime storage-region selector or DPA found in product/docs/FAQ/security pages. GitHub privacy covers processing in multiple locations, including the US and other operating countries, and describes processor relationships under a DPA.

facts.label: Product identity
facts.value: Upptime; official site upptime.js.org and template repository github.com/upptime/upptime. Created by an individual maintainer. No former product name identified.

facts.label: Availability and changes
facts.value: Upstream template is not archived or disabled. Latest monitor release returned is v1.46.5, published 2026-10-25; it includes a nodemailer security dependency update. No whole-product shutdown, sunset or acquisition notice found.

facts.label: Software license and source
facts.value: MIT License; official source/template github.com/upptime/upptime, plus monitor and status-page component repositories.

facts.label: History-data license
facts.value: The template separately labels history-directory data under the Open Database License (ODbL); it has its own history/LICENSE file.

facts.label: Help and support
facts.value: Public docs, GitHub issues/discussions and responsible security contact opensource@anandchowdhary.com. No paid Upptime support entitlement, response-time contract or fixed support hours found.

facts.label: Updates and security
facts.value: Current template-update schedule is daily and calls the updater from master; docs say not to hand-edit generated workflows. Security policy asks users to monitor releases and patch, with private disclosure via security contact.

facts.label: Backup and restore
facts.value: Back up config and committed history with git, and account separately for GitHub issues/comments, repository settings, secrets and other platform data. GitHub's backup guide provides mirror-repository restore guidance but warns metadata archives have different limits.

facts.value: Use service.version and Sentry release attributes; CI/CD can post chart annotations with commit links and deduplication fingerprint. Error alerts close manually and similar patterns can alert again.

facts.value: Trace-linked logs/errors, attributes, nearby log context and Sentry breadcrumbs; user context can be attached through SDKs. Stack/detail panels appear only if data is supplied.

facts.label: Session replay
facts.value: Sentry integration page includes optional replayIntegration configuration, but no Uptrace replay viewer, compatible event coverage, retention or replay quota/price was established in the checked feature docs.

facts.label: HTTP check types
facts.value: Collector HTTP receiver supports HTTP methods, body, headers, content/JSON-path/regex/size assertions and localhost targets. Uptrace receives exported result metrics.

facts.label: Frequency
facts.value: Uptrace example runs HTTP checks every 60 seconds; upstream receiver default is 60 seconds with configurable duration. Cloud metrics minimum supported interval is 10 seconds.

facts.label: Timeout and minimum
facts.value: No Uptrace-specific per-check timeout or shortest supported Collector HTTP interval published in the checked guide. Upstream config embeds OpenTelemetry HTTP ClientConfig; actual timeout depends on Collector version/config.

facts.label: Probe locations and counting
facts.value: Run the Collector where checks should originate, including a private network. No vendor-managed probe inventory or per-run tariff established; resulting metric datapoints consume telemetry allowance.

facts.label: Failure confirmation and maintenance
facts.value: Guide recommends monitoring over two to three collection intervals to reduce transient alerts; Uptrace monitors can be muted for a chosen duration. No managed multi-location quorum or billable retry policy found.

facts.label: Certificate and domain expiry
facts.value: Optional receiver metric httpcheck.tls.cert_remaining supports certificate warnings; guide example alerts below 2,592,000 seconds, or 30 days. Receiver TLS metrics must be enabled.

facts.label: Searching and log detail
facts.value: Grouped/raw log views, time histogram, full-text AND/OR/exclusions and attribute-scoped search, regex/range filters, severity/service filters and trace correlation.

facts.label: Cold archives
facts.value: Cloud advertises S3/HDD cold retention up to 100 weeks; restore process, retrieval latency/fee and equivalent normal searchable history were not published in pricing or log docs.

facts.label: Slow requests and service links
facts.value: Trace waterfall, p50/p90/p99 latency, request/error rates, formatted database queries, span comparisons and automatic service graph from related client/server spans.

facts.label: Profiling depth
facts.value: No first-party continuous CPU/heap profiling ingestion, flamegraph retention or separate profiling price established in feature, tracing and Swift docs.

facts.label: Sampling
facts.value: Go distribution samples all traces by default; configure SDK head sampling. Server transformation sample fraction is 0 to 1 and can keep error spans while sampling successful traffic.

facts.label: Real-user performance
facts.value: Browser SDK instruments Fetch, XMLHttpRequest and document load; custom user interactions and page-load metrics documented. Swift supports Apple platform tracing/metrics and URLSession instrumentation.

facts.label: Dependencies and initial sizing
facts.value: ClickHouse 26.3+, PostgreSQL 15+ and Redis required. Docker guide minimum: 2+ CPU cores, 4+ GB RAM and 10+ GB disk for initial setup.

facts.label: Production capacity
facts.value: Scaling guide suggests Uptrace instance 2–4 CPU / 4–8 GB, PostgreSQL 2–4 CPU / 4–8 GB and Redis 1–2 CPU / 2–4 GB; ClickHouse capacity depends on telemetry/storage workload.

facts.label: Muting and incident workflow
facts.value: Monitors can be muted temporarily or open alerts closed manually. Incidents group alerts and track assignment/notes/status; automatic grouping/analysis requires a configured generative model client.

facts.label: Retrieving and moving data
facts.value: Log/trace details expose JSON; dashboards export/import YAML; MCP list/get tools query individual records and aggregates.

facts.label: Cancellation deletion
facts.value: Cloud content becomes inaccessible immediately on cancellation, removed from active systems/logs within 30 days and backups within 60 days.

facts.label: Self-host deletion and recovery scope
facts.value: Database reset/truncate commands can remove telemetry; owner controls their databases and backups. Privacy portability rights do not document an unlimited telemetry export API.

facts.label: Filtering and redaction
facts.value: Server transformations can delete/keep attributes and drop records. Sentry beforeSend example removes user email before export; browser instrumentation supports ignored request URLs.

facts.label: Encryption policy
facts.value: Privacy says browser transport is SSL/TLS, database backups encrypted, but most live database data is not encrypted at rest.

facts.label: Self-host security
facts.value: Generated random service secret, database credentials, TLS, authentication restrictions and firewall configuration documented; premium options include SSO, 2FA and RBAC by edition.

facts.label: Storage regions
facts.value: Cloud pricing names Hetzner Germany for primary data and Finland for redundant backups; privacy says transfer/storage in Germany. Self-host owner chooses infrastructure.

facts.value: No documented complete bulk raw-telemetry export, export size/rate limit or archive egress tariff found in MCP, log details, configuration or portability policy; guessed /api page returned 404.

facts.value: Active Cloud and self-hosted offers. Latest release API returns v2.1.0-rc.2, published 2026-10-22; tag contains rc although prerelease=false.

facts.value: No whole-product shutdown, sunset or acquisition notice found in the checked official blog index, news posts, repository release and status page; /newsroom returned HTTP 404.

facts.label: Data retention
facts.value: Public status pages show a rolling 30-day uptime strip, incident history for 7 days after resolution, and automatically recorded up/down events for 90 days, up to 50 entries.

facts.label: Data retention
facts.value: Reports page says report data is retained while the account is active and offers 7-, 30-, or 90-day report windows.

facts.label: People, apps, and projects

facts.label: People, apps, and projects
facts.value: Checks: Free 20, Starter 75, Pro 250, Business 1,000. Port and domain monitors do not count against this check allowance.

facts.label: Home region and eligible buyers
facts.value: No supported-country or buyer-eligibility list was found in Terms, Privacy, pricing, or About.

facts.label: Jobs it covers
facts.value: Heartbeat monitoring for scheduled jobs and background tasks; HTTP/HTTPS site and API uptime; TCP, UDP, DNS, and ICMP checks; SSL expiry; domain expiry; IP blocklist monitoring; scheduled HTTP calls through Cloud Cron; incidents and public status pages.

facts.label: Jobs it covers
facts.value: Product pages checked do not document exception capture, searchable application logs, distributed traces, application performance monitoring, or browser-session replay.

facts.label: Hosted and self-hosted options
facts.value: The standard Free, Starter, Pro, and Business plans are presented as a hosted WatchCron service. Enterprise pricing also says “Self-hosted regions on request,” but does not explain whether customers operate a complete deployment or what “regions” means.

facts.label: Languages and frameworks
facts.value: No SDK or language-specific agent is required for heartbeat checks: any environment able to make an HTTP request can call the ping URL. Official examples cover Bash, PHP, Node.js, Python, Go, GitHub Actions, and Docker; docs also list Ruby, PowerShell, Laravel, WordPress, and systemd examples.

facts.label: Alert channels and costs
facts.value: Current pricing card sets channel caps at 3 for Free, 10 Starter, 25 Pro, and unlimited Business. Pricing table lists Slack, Telegram, PagerDuty, and 16 more across all plans; SMS is Pro and Business, while voice and WhatsApp are Business.

facts.label: Alert channels and costs
facts.value: Feature article says email and webhooks are available on all plans; Starter adds Slack, Telegram, Discord, and Teams; Pro adds SMS; Business adds voice, PagerDuty, and OpsGenie. It says no per-alert fees or alert-volume caps.

facts.label: Alert channels and costs
facts.value: Homepage says “22 channels”; pricing card says “3 channels · 19 types” for Free. The pages do not explain how channel caps, channel types, or the 22-channel headline relate.

facts.label: Alert noise and escalation
facts.value: Cron monitors support an alert-after consecutive-miss threshold, per-check maintenance windows, repeat notifications off by default, and configurable repeat intervals.

facts.label: Alert noise and escalation
facts.value: Multi-channel alerts route by project and can be selected per monitor; alerts fire on down and recovery. PagerDuty and OpsGenie integrations hand off escalation to those services on the Business plan according to the detailed alert article.

facts.label: Alert noise and escalation
facts.value: The channel article says WatchCron itself does not provide on-call rotation or alert deduplication; it relies on PagerDuty or OpsGenie for formal escalation schedules.

facts.label: Deployment fit
facts.value: Hosted browser dashboard; no monitoring agent is required. Heartbeat monitors work with any job environment that can make an outbound HTTP request.

facts.label: Deployment fit
facts.value: Cloud Cron calls publicly accessible URLs from WatchCron infrastructure. Private-network endpoints are not supported unless the user exposes or tunnels them; jobs needing more than 60 seconds should run elsewhere and report a heartbeat.

facts.label: Deployment fit
facts.value: Public status pages are hosted at watchcron.com/status/<slug>; private or password-protected status pages are not documented.

facts.label: Sending data in
facts.value: Heartbeat data is sent by HTTP GET or POST to a unique ping URL; optional POST body can be up to 100 KB. Ping endpoints include success, start, fail, and log paths.

facts.label: Sending data in
facts.value: A REST API manages checks and retrieves ping history and status flips. Current API documentation says full API coverage is for cron/heartbeat checks; HTTP, port, SSL, domain, blocklist, incidents, and status-page APIs are not yet covered.

facts.label: Sending data in
facts.value: No OpenTelemetry, syslog, log, metric, or trace ingestion endpoint is documented in the product pages or docs index checked.

facts.label: Setup path
facts.value: For a heartbeat check: create a check, name it and define a cron expression or interval, set grace, copy the unique ping URL, add an HTTP request to the job, then configure and assign alert channels.

facts.label: Setup path
facts.value: For Cloud Cron: create a job with a public target URL, method, cron expression, timezone, timeout, optional headers/body/auth, retry count, and alert channels.

facts.label: Uptime check types
facts.value: HTTP/HTTPS checks monitor URL reachability, expected status code, response time, and optional required/forbidden text. HTTPS certificate expiry is checked with uptime monitoring.

facts.label: Uptime check types
facts.value: Network monitors support TCP, UDP, DNS record types A/AAAA/MX/CNAME/TXT/NS, and ICMP. DNS monitors can compare returned values with an expected value.

facts.label: Uptime check types
facts.value: External HTTP monitor authentication and private-network support are not fully specified in the uptime page checked. Cloud Cron supports HTTP Basic Auth but that is a separate scheduled-request feature.

facts.label: Uptime check frequency and timeout
facts.value: Current homepage says HTTP checks can run as often as every 30 seconds; the uptime page says five minutes by default, configurable to run more or less often, with the same frequency on every plan.

facts.label: Uptime check frequency and timeout
facts.value: HTTP response timeout defaults to 10 seconds; a timeout counts as a failed check.

facts.label: Uptime check frequency and timeout
facts.value: Port checks default to 5 minutes with a 10-second timeout; minimum intervals are Free 5 minutes, Starter 1 minute, Pro and Business 30 seconds. Timeout can be set from 1 to 60 seconds.

facts.label: Probe locations and check counting
facts.value: HTTP checks run from one location, with no multi-region confirmation; no alternate locations or private probes are documented.

facts.label: Probe locations and check counting
facts.value: One URL is counted as one check regardless of interval; channels and team members do not count. Port and domain monitors are separate quotas and do not count against checks.

facts.label: Failure confirmation and maintenance
facts.value: Uptime feature page describes a single-location failure with no multi-region confirmation. It does not publish a retry or consecutive-failure rule before HTTP alerts.

facts.label: Failure confirmation and maintenance
facts.value: A user-configured maintenance pause for HTTP checks was not found on the uptime page or status-page documentation checked.

facts.label: Certificate and domain expiry
facts.value: SSL expiry warning window is configurable from 1 to 90 days, default 14 days; alerts repeat daily until renewal and do not change site up/down status.

facts.label: Certificate and domain expiry
facts.value: WHOIS domain checks run twice daily; expiry warning is configurable from 1 to 365 days, default 30, with an alert on entering the window and another if the domain expires.

facts.label: Schedule and grace rules
facts.value: Cron heartbeat checks accept simple interval schedules or a full cron expression, with a per-check timezone and a Next 5 Runs preview. Default grace is five minutes and is configurable per job; a consecutive-miss threshold is available.

facts.label: Schedule and grace rules
facts.value: Cloud Cron uses cron expressions, IANA timezones, and accounts for daylight-saving transitions; minimum schedule interval is one minute and request timeout range is 1–60 seconds.

facts.label: Schedule and grace rules
facts.value: Duration threshold can flag a job that runs too long; cron monitors support per-check maintenance windows and repeat-notification intervals.

facts.label: Job failure signals
facts.value: Success ping detects a completed run; /start begins duration timing; /fail marks the job down immediately; /log attaches up to 100 KB of output. Missing expected pings are checked every minute.

facts.label: Job failure signals
facts.value: Ping history and state flips are available through the REST API; privacy says ping retention follows subscription limits but does not give durations by plan.

facts.label: Status-page limits and branding
facts.value: Public status pages are included on every plan, one page per project; project quotas are Free 2, Starter 5, Pro 20, Business unlimited. Subscriber count is unlimited.

facts.label: Status-page limits and branding
facts.value: Pages use watchcron.com/status/<slug>; no own domain, logo, color theme, favicon, or private/password-protected mode is available according to the detailed page.

facts.label: Subscriber notifications
facts.value: Customers subscribe by verified email; every incident open, update, and resolution sends email. Automatic monitor blips are visible but do not email subscribers.

facts.label: Status update source
facts.value: Overall page state is calculated from cron/heartbeat, HTTP uptime, and port/network monitor states. Domain expiry, blocklist, and SSL monitors are excluded from the public status page.

facts.label: Status update source
facts.value: Operators can publish incidents manually through Investigating, Identified, Monitoring, and Resolved states with timestamped updates. Resolved incidents remain for 7 days; automatic up/down history is 90 days, up to 50 entries.

facts.label: Self-host requirements
facts.value: Enterprise pricing says “Self-hosted regions on request,” but no installation, architecture, database, resource-sizing, or deployment guide was found.

facts.label: Export and deletion
facts.value: REST API exposes ping history and status flips as JSON; reports can be exported as PDF or CSV, and a read-only report link can be shared.

facts.label: Export and deletion
facts.value: Users can export monitoring data in a portable format and delete personal data through settings or by contacting the vendor; account personal data is removed within 30 days, subject to legal retention.

facts.label: Export and deletion
facts.value: Deleting a check permanently erases its associated ping records.

facts.label: Sensitive-data controls
facts.value: Ping payloads and Cloud Cron request headers/bodies may carry user-supplied content; privacy states that optional monitoring ping bodies are collected. A documented body limit is 100 KB.

facts.label: Sensitive-data controls
facts.value: Redaction, field masking, exclusion rules, and retention controls for sensitive ping or Cloud Cron request data are not specified in the privacy, API, or product pages checked.

facts.label: Storage regions and data terms
facts.value: Storage location and region selection for monitoring data are not stated in Privacy or Terms. Enterprise pricing offers a signed DPA and “self-hosted regions on request,” without public terms or region details.

facts.label: Product identity
facts.value: WatchCron; canonical site https://watchcron.com/. Current pages do not identify a former name.

facts.value: Current homepage, plans, and public registration links advertise a live hosted service and invite new users.

facts.label: Availability and product changes
facts.value: Homepage footer reports “All systems operational”; the separate status endpoint could not be checked.

facts.label: Availability and product changes
facts.value: No WatchCron acquisition, sunset, or shutdown announcement was found in the official homepage, About, Terms, Privacy, and blog items checked.

facts.value: A blog post dated Oct 24, 2026 discusses Cronhub's shutdown and migration to WatchCron.

facts.label: License and code
facts.value: No public source repository or license for the complete WatchCron service was linked from the product, docs, or pricing pages checked.

facts.label: Help and documentation
facts.value: Public documentation index and feature guides are available; About lists a contact page and email for questions. No contractual standard response time was found for ordinary plans.

facts.label: Help and documentation
facts.value: Enterprise plan includes a contractual response time, SSO/SAML, signed DPA, invoicing, and higher check volumes. Price is not public; pricing directs buyers to contact sales.

facts.label: Self-host upkeep
facts.value: Upgrade, backup, restore, and security procedures for a possible self-hosted deployment are not documented in the public docs index or product pages checked.

facts.label: Business price
facts.value: EUR 73/month; USD 78/month; GBP 65/month, excluding VAT.

facts.label: Enterprise billing
facts.value: Custom price, invoiced billing, and 10,000 checks are listed. Currency and commitment depend on a quote and are not published.

facts.label: Cancellation
facts.value: Self-serve subscriptions can be cancelled in billing settings or Paddle's management flow. Cancellation stops future renewals; the current period is not automatically refunded.

facts.label: Ongoing free plan
facts.value: Free indefinitely, no card, 10 checks, unlimited projects, one user and 200 ping-log entries.

facts.label: Free-plan commercial use
facts.value: Pricing describes Free as for individuals and side projects. Whether it permits commercial use is not expressly stated in the checked pricing or Terms pages.

facts.label: Open Source program

facts.label: Business allowances

facts.label: Smallest useful paid plan

facts.label: Check-count limit behavior
facts.value: Each plan has a maximum check count. Auto-provisioning respects the plan cap; when the account is at or above it, check creation returns HTTP 403. No automatic paid overage is described.

facts.label: Notification quotas
facts.value: SMS, WhatsApp and calls have plan-based monthly quotas that reset monthly and do not roll over. Exceeding them triggers a warning email and an Integrations-page warning. What happens to additional sends or whether they incur a charge is not stated.

facts.label: Ping-log limit
facts.value: The pricing page lists 200, 1,500, 3,000 and 10,000 ping-log entries across Free, Startup, Business and Enterprise. Whether this is total retained history or a per-check limit is not explained.

facts.label: Notification behavior after quota
facts.value: After the monthly SMS, WhatsApp or call allowance is exceeded, docs promise an email and dashboard warning but do not say whether sends stop, queue, or create charges.

facts.label: Bill controls
facts.value: No user-set hard spend cap, usage-based spending alert, or per-project bill stop is documented. Public self-serve plans are fixed subscriptions, but Enterprise uses a quote.

facts.label: Data retention — Free ping history
facts.value: Free lists 200 ping-log entries.

facts.label: Data retention — Startup ping history
facts.value: Startup lists 1,500 ping-log entries.

facts.label: Data retention — Business ping history
facts.value: Business lists 3,000 ping-log entries.

facts.label: Data retention — Enterprise ping history
facts.value: Enterprise lists 10,000 ping-log entries.

facts.label: Ping-history duration and scope
facts.value: Expiration period and whether entry counts apply per account or per check are not stated in the pricing, docs or privacy policy checked.

facts.label: Data retention — account and project data
facts.value: Account and project data are kept while the account is active. Billing, tax, entitlement and security/audit records may be kept longer for legal, accounting, fraud or dispute needs; backups rotate and are not an active archive.

facts.label: Free check and project allowance
facts.value: 10 checks and unlimited projects.

facts.label: Startup check and project allowance
facts.value: 100 checks and unlimited projects.

facts.label: Business check and project allowance
facts.value: 1,000 checks and unlimited projects.

facts.label: Enterprise check and project allowance
facts.value: 10,000 checks and unlimited projects.

facts.label: Users and team access
facts.value: Free includes one user. Startup, Business and Enterprise include team access and project roles. A numeric paid seat limit or seat price is not published.

facts.label: Numeric paid seat limit
facts.value: A maximum number of paid team members per project/account and any extra-seat price are not published.

facts.label: Log allowances and loss
facts.value: For job output attached to a ping, the API stores up to the first 10 kB of the request body. The plan page also lists ping-log entry counts, but their scope and expiry behavior are not defined.

facts.label: Query and extra-data charges
facts.value: Not applicable as a separate log product: public plans meter checks and show log-entry allowances, but no query or byte-based log fee is listed. Enterprise pricing is custom.

facts.label: Home region
facts.value: Watchgoose says it is headquartered in the United Kingdom; its own description says hosting and operations are in Europe. Legal entity: Pixeware LTD, UK.

facts.label: Eligible buyers
facts.value: No buyer-country eligibility list was found on the pricing, Terms or Privacy pages.

facts.label: Jobs it covers
facts.value: Heartbeat and missed-run monitoring for cron jobs, backups, scripts, queues, systemd timers and CI workflows. A check can alert on an explicit failure or a missing expected success. Optional public pages communicate selected check states.

facts.label: Scope boundary
facts.value: Watchgoose says it is not intended for website uptime probing, application-performance metrics or general log aggregation.

facts.label: Hosted and self-hosted options
facts.value: Vendor-hosted service. Official docs describe account-based use of Watchgoose; no complete self-hosted server distribution or installation guide was found.

facts.label: Languages and frameworks
facts.value: No SDK is required: any job able to make an HTTP request or send email can report. Official examples cover shell, systemd, GitHub Actions and language-specific request examples; this is protocol compatibility, not a list of maintained SDKs.

facts.label: Alert channels
facts.value: Official pages describe email, webhooks, SMS, WhatsApp, phone calls, chat and incident-management integrations; examples name Slack, PagerDuty, Splunk On-Call, Opsgenie, PagerTree and Pushover. Marketing says 12+ channels.

facts.label: Startup SMS and call allowance
facts.value: 50 SMS and 20 phone calls each month.

facts.label: Business SMS and call allowance
facts.value: 500 SMS and 100 phone calls each month.

facts.label: Enterprise SMS and call allowance
facts.value: 1,000 SMS and 500 phone calls each month.

facts.label: Free SMS and call allowance
facts.value: The Free plan's monthly SMS, WhatsApp and phone-call quotas are not shown in pricing.

facts.label: Email and other delivery cost
facts.value: Email, chat and webhooks are included in plan descriptions; no separate fee is listed. SMS/WhatsApp/call quotas are distinct. Any extra-send price is not published.

facts.label: Alert routing and repeats
facts.value: Multiple integrations can be assigned to a project and toggled per check. Hourly or daily email reminders can repeat while any check is down. Escalation rules for PagerDuty and other incident systems are configured there, not described as Watchgoose escalation tiers.

facts.label: Alert grouping, acknowledgement and delay controls
facts.value: No alert grouping, in-product acknowledgement workflow, or per-alert delay/escalation schedule was found in the checked notification and check-configuration docs.

facts.label: Deployment fit
facts.value: Fits scheduled work on machines or workflows that can reach Watchgoose over HTTP or email. Official guides cover cron, systemd timers, GitHub Actions and shell scripts; no agent install is required.

facts.label: Agent and runtime requirement
facts.value: No Watchgoose agent or SDK is needed. The documented setup adds an HTTP call or sends an email from the job; examples use curl/wget and language HTTP clients.

facts.label: Data sent in
facts.value: HTTP ping API accepts HEAD, GET and POST and supports success, start, failure, exit-code and status-neutral log signals. Each check can also receive email pings at a unique address.

facts.label: Project management API
facts.value: Project-scoped API can list, create, update, pause, resume and delete checks; list pings and status changes; and retrieve a logged ping body. It is rate-limited to 100 requests/minute, after which HTTP 429 can occur.

facts.label: Setup path
facts.value: Create a check, select a simple/cron/OnCalendar schedule and grace period, add an HTTP ping or unique email address to the job, then configure its notification integrations.

facts.label: Error grouping and coverage
facts.value: Not applicable: the product monitors scheduled-job signals, not application exceptions.

facts.label: Readable error locations
facts.value: Not applicable: no exception stack-trace or source-map product is offered.

facts.label: Release and fix tracking
facts.value: Not applicable: no application error release-tracking feature is offered.

facts.label: Context and replay
facts.value: Not applicable: no user-session replay or application error context feature is offered.

facts.label: Check types
facts.value: Not applicable to general uptime/synthetic checks. Docs say Watchgoose is not for probing website uptime; it monitors jobs that send a heartbeat.

facts.label: Check frequency and timeout
facts.value: Not applicable to outside uptime checks. Job schedule and grace are recorded under J01.

facts.label: Probe locations and check counting
facts.value: Not applicable: no outside probe network is offered for website checks. Job checks are counted against account plan limits.

facts.label: Failure confirmation and maintenance
facts.value: Not applicable to synthetic website probes. Job grace periods and pause controls are documented separately.

facts.label: Certificate and domain expiry
facts.value: Not applicable: no certificate/domain-expiry checks are offered in the reviewed product docs.

facts.label: Status-page limits and access
facts.value: One basic public page per project, available on all plans, disabled by default, with an opaque Watchgoose URL. Each page can show 1–100 checks. Visitors do not need an account.

facts.label: Status-page page text and styling
facts.value: Owners can set a title, plain-text description, public names and groups. HTML, Markdown, links and custom CSS are not interpreted.

facts.label: Custom domain and branded URL
facts.value: The page uses an opaque Watchgoose URL. Custom domains or alternate branded URLs are not described.

facts.label: Subscriber notifications
facts.value: The public page is viewable without an account, but subscriber registration and email/SMS page-update notifications are not described in status-page or pricing docs.

facts.label: Status update source
facts.value: Page components show the current state and age of the selected checks. Status changes therefore follow the monitored job signals automatically.

facts.label: Manual incidents and history
facts.value: Manual incident announcements, maintenance notices and public incident-history duration are not described in the status-page docs.

facts.label: Schedule and grace rules
facts.value: Simple period, five-field Cron and systemd OnCalendar schedules are supported. The check is late at its expected schedule; the configured grace time delays the Down alert. Time zone is configurable for cron/OnCalendar jobs.

facts.label: Cron syntax limits
facts.value: Five-field cron expressions are accepted. The current Node-cron guide says seconds and W are unsupported; when both day-of-month and day-of-week are set, Watchgoose follows crontab's either-field behavior.

facts.label: Shortest simple interval
facts.value: The current Node-cron guide says the shortest simple-period check is 60 seconds; six-field second-level cron expressions are not accepted.

facts.label: Time-zone and DST handling
facts.value: The user can set the server time zone and the docs warn that a mismatch shifts expected pings. Specific daylight-saving transition behavior is not stated in the docs checked.

facts.label: Job failure signals
facts.value: A successful ping confirms a completed run; a missing success after its schedule and grace triggers Down. Jobs can send /fail or a nonzero exit code for immediate failure, and /start plus success records duration and alerts on a run exceeding grace.

facts.label: Job output and log signals
